THOUGHT: This 17-year-old male presents with acute, severe left wrist monoarthritis (swelling, erythema, profound tenderness to palpation and passive motion), systemic symptoms (fever [37.7°C], chills, malaise), and characteristic skin findings: painless violaceous vesiculopustular lesions on both wrists and hands — a classic dermatologic manifestation of disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI). The recent history of self-resolving knee pain one week prior is highly suggestive of migratory polyarthralgia/arthritis, another hallmark of DGI. His sexual activity with a single partner (inadequate barrier protection given diaphragm use only) and positive NAAT for *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* (with negative chlamydia and HIV) strongly support gonococcal etiology. Critically, joint aspiration reveals >50,000 WBC/μL (indicating septic arthritis) and Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci — pathognomonic for *N. gonorrhoeae* (though culture confirmation is ideal, Gram stain in this clinical context is highly specific). While Lyme disease is endemic in Minnesota and can cause arthritis, it does not present with vesiculopustular skin lesions, acute purulent monoarthritis with gram-negative diplococci on stain, or gonorrhea-positive STI testing. Reactive arthritis (e.g., post-chlamydial) is unlikely given negative chlamydia and presence of active gonococcal infection plus classic DGI skin and joint findings. The absence of trauma, normal baseline health, and temporal association with recent sexual exposure further narrow the diagnosis.

DIAGNOSIS: Disseminated gonococcal infection
